Series::erfinv¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::erfinv() const
Series& Series::erfinv_()

What It Does¶

Computes the inverse error function elementwise. erfinv is the functional inverse of erf on the open interval (-1, 1):

erf( erfinv(x) ) = x        for x in (-1, 1)

Its main use is turning a uniform or probability-scale quantity into a Gaussian one. The standard-normal quantile function is a rescaled erfinv:

Phi^{-1}(p) = sqrt(2) * erfinv(2p - 1)

so drawing p uniformly and passing it through this relation produces standard-normal samples, and mapping model probabilities back to a latent Gaussian scale (a probit link) is the same operation.

Domain and endpoints:

  • erfinv(0) = 0.

  • erfinv is odd: erfinv(-x) = -erfinv(x).

  • As x -> 1 the value goes to +inf; as x -> -1 it goes to -inf. erfinv(1) returns +inf and erfinv(-1) returns -inf exactly.

  • Outside [-1, 1] the inverse does not exist. erfinv(x) returns NaN there — it does not clamp the argument back into range.

erfinv() is out-of-place; erfinv_() overwrites the current storage. The forward value is computed from a rational approximation refined by two Newton steps against erf, accurate to near machine precision on the interior.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

Series or Series& A Series with the same shape as self. Interior arguments map to finite values, +/-1 to +/-inf, and |x| > 1 to NaN. erfinv_() returns a reference to the mutated series.

An integral input is promoted to float64.

Gradient¶

erfinv() is differentiable on the interior. By the inverse-function rule, with y = erfinv(x) and erf'(y) = (2/sqrt(pi)) e^(-y^2):

d/dx erfinv(x) = sqrt(pi)/2 * exp( erfinv(x)^2 )

The derivative is sqrt(pi)/2 = 0.8862 at x = 0 and grows without bound toward the endpoints. At x = +/-1 the forward value is infinite and the sensitivity is +inf; for |x| > 1 both are NaN.

Examples¶

Example 1. Interior values, including the odd symmetry.

pluss::series::print(std::cout,
                     pluss::make_series({0.0, 0.5, -0.5, 0.9}).erfinv());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 0.4769, -0.4769, 1.1631]

Example 2. It inverts erf: erf(erfinv(x)) returns x.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-0.8, -0.2, 0.3, 0.95}).erfinv().erf());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.8000, -0.2000, 0.3000, 0.9500]

Example 3. Endpoints and out-of-domain arguments. +/-1 give +/-inf; any |x| > 1 gives NaN. The argument is never silently clamped.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({1.0, -1.0, 1.5, 2.0, -2.0}).erfinv()
) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[inf, -inf, nan, nan, nan]

Example 4. The backward pass is sqrt(pi)/2 * exp(erfinv(x)^2) — smallest at the centre, rising toward the endpoints.

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.0, 0.3, 0.6});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.erfinv().sum().reverse();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.8862, 0.9545, 1.2629]

Example 5. Integral inputs are promoted to float64. Note that 1 is an endpoint, so the promoted result is +inf.

pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({0, 1}).erfinv());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, inf]

Example 6. erfinv_() overwrites the current storage in place.

auto a = pluss::make_series({0.0, 0.5, 1.0});
a.erfinv_();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a);

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 0.4769, inf]

Example 7. Convert central probabilities to standard-normal quantiles. The affine step maps [0, 1] to the error-function domain [-1, 1]; the final sqrt(2) changes from the error-function scale to standard deviations.

auto probabilities = pluss::make_series({0.025, 0.5, 0.975});
auto quantiles = probabilities.mul(2.0)
                              .sub(1.0)
                              .erfinv()
                              .mul(std::sqrt(2.0));
pluss::series::print(std::cout, quantiles) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.9600, 0.0000, 1.9600]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Arguments outside [-1, 1] return NaN; the method never silently clamps invalid input. If a probability-scale quantity can acquire small rounding excursions, validate or clamp it deliberately before calling.

  • erfinv(+/-1) is +/-inf, not a finite sentinel.

  • The gradient blows up near the endpoints; a tracked erfinv() on data close to +/-1 produces very large sensitivities.

  • For the standard-normal quantile use sqrt(2) * erfinv(2p - 1); erfinv itself is on the erf scale, not the Phi scale.

  • Integral inputs promote to float64.

  • erfinv_() requires floating storage. Use erfinv() when starting from an integral series so the result has somewhere to store fractional values.

Summary¶

erfinv() inverts erf on (-1, 1):

  • erfinv(0) = 0, odd, erfinv(+/-1) = +/-inf

  • |x| > 1 returns NaN — no clamping

  • differentiable on the interior with backward sqrt(pi)/2 * exp(erfinv(x)^2)

  • the normal quantile is sqrt(2) * erfinv(2p - 1)

  • erfinv_() is the in-place form

See Also¶

  • Series::erf: the function this inverts.

  • Series::erfcinv: the inverse of the complementary error function, better conditioned in the far tail.

  • Series::erfc: the complementary error function.
